chapter_summary:
Effective user and group management is the cornerstone of a secure and well-administered Linux system. While basic `useradd` and `groupadd` commands are fundamental, an LFCE needs to understand the underlying mechanisms and advanced options to handle complex enterprise scenarios. Every user and group on a Linux system is identified by a unique numerical ID: UID for users and GID for groups. These IDs are critical because they are what the kernel actually uses to identify ownership and permissions, not the human-readable names. This becomes particularly important in networked environments where consistent UIDs/GIDs across multiple systems prevent permission issues and simplify data sharing. For instance, if a user `devuser` has UID 1001 on Server A and UID 1005 on Server B, files owned by `devuser` on Server A will appear to be owned by a different user (or nobody) on Server B if that UID 1001 isn't mapped correctly.

When creating users, beyond simply providing a username, you often need to specify a home directory, a default shell, a primary group, and potentially secondary groups. The `useradd` command offers a wealth of options for this. For example, to create a system user for a specific application, you might use `useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin -d /opt/appdata appuser`. The `-r` flag creates a system account, typically with a UID below 1000, which is useful for services that don't need interactive logins. The `-s /sbin/nologin` prevents login altogether, a crucial security measure for service accounts. The `-d` flag specifies a custom home directory, which might be necessary if the application expects its configuration or data in a non-standard location. Understanding the difference between primary and secondary groups is also vital. Every user must belong to a primary group, which is typically created with the same name as the user by default. Secondary groups grant additional permissions, often for shared resources or project-based access. You can add a user to secondary groups during creation with `-G` or later with `usermod -aG`.

The core configuration files for users and groups are `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/group`, and `/etc/gshadow`. `/etc/passwd` contains user account information, including username, UID, GID, home directory, and default shell, but importantly, no password hash. The password hash is stored securely in `/etc/shadow`, which is only readable by root. This separation is a critical security feature. `/etc/group` lists group names and their GIDs, along with a list of users who are members of that group. Similarly, `/etc/gshadow` stores encrypted passwords for groups (though group passwords are less commonly used) and group administrators. As an LFCE, you should be able to parse these files manually for troubleshooting or auditing, although direct editing is generally discouraged in favor of command-line tools like `usermod`, `groupmod`, and `gpasswd`.

Beyond basic creation, managing existing users involves tasks like changing passwords (`passwd`), modifying user attributes (`usermod`), and deleting users (`userdel`). When deleting a user, you must decide whether to remove their home directory and mail spool, which `userdel -r` handles. However, files outside the home directory owned by the deleted user will remain, and their ownership will show as the deleted UID. This orphaned ownership can be a security risk or simply lead to confusion, requiring a strategy to reassign or remove such files. For instance, you might use `find / -uid <deleted_UID> -exec chown newuser:newgroup {} \;` to reassign ownership.

Common mistakes include not setting appropriate default shells for service accounts, leading to potential login vulnerabilities, or failing to remove a user's home directory and data, which can leave sensitive information exposed. Another frequent error is inconsistent UID/GID management across multiple systems, causing permission headaches in shared storage environments like NFS. Always strive for consistency, especially for critical service accounts. Security best practices also dictate implementing account expiration (`chage -E YYYY-MM-DD username`) and locking accounts (`passwd -l username`) for inactive users or after multiple failed login attempts, which we will explore further in later chapters. The `/etc/login.defs` file defines system-wide defaults for user creation, such as the default UID/GID ranges, password aging parameters, and umask values. Understanding and customizing these defaults can significantly streamline user management and enforce security policies across the system.

```bash
# Example: Creating a system user for a web application with specific settings
sudo useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin -d /var/www/mywebapp -c "My WebApp Service User" mywebapp
# Verify user creation and attributes
id mywebapp
grep mywebapp /etc/passwd
grep mywebapp /etc/shadow

# Example: Creating a new group for project members
sudo groupadd project_alpha

# Example: Adding an existing user to a secondary group
sudo usermod -aG project_alpha john_doe

# Example: Changing a user's default shell and primary group
# First, create a new primary group for the user if needed
sudo groupadd devops_team
# Then, change the user's primary group and shell
sudo usermod -g devops_team -s /bin/bash jane_doe

# Example: Setting an account expiration date
sudo chage -E 2024-12-31 john_doe

# Example: Deleting a user and their home directory
sudo userdel -r olduser
```

screens.title: Advanced User and Group Management
screens.subtitle: UIDs, GIDs, service accounts, and secure lifecycle controls

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on why numerical IDs and careful account configuration matter in production systems. You will learn how the kernel uses UIDs and GIDs rather than names, and why consistent IDs across servers prevent permission surprises when sharing files. We will also cover advanced user creation flags, how to set up non-interactive system accounts, and how to manage account lifecycle with expiration and locking. A concrete example you will see is creating a system service user with no login and a dedicated data directory, then verifying its attributes with the id command and by inspecting system files. Common mistakes like inconsistent UIDs across NFS mounts or leaving orphaned files after deletion will be highlighted so you can avoid them. By the end of this chapter you will be able to create, modify, and retire users and groups in a consistent and auditable way, and you will understand which files to check when troubleshooting ownership and access issues.

keyIdea.title: Why numeric IDs matter
keyIdea.text: UIDs and GIDs are the kernel’s source of truth for ownership. Consistency across systems preserves permissions and prevents orphaned ownership.

narration.text: These objectives focus on the core knowledge and practical skills you will build. First, you'll understand UIDs and GIDs: why the kernel uses numeric IDs and how inconsistent IDs across servers cause permission problems. For example, a developer's UID that differs between two hosts can make files seem to belong to another account when mounted over shared storage. Second, you'll master the command-line tools for creating, modifying, and deleting users and groups with specific attributes. That means using useradd to set shells, home directories, and primary and secondary groups, and using usermod and groupmod to alter attributes safely. Each objective is practical: by the end you should be able to create a non-interactive system account, add users to secondary groups, and delete accounts while choosing whether to remove home directories. A common misconception to watch for is assuming usernames alone govern access; they do not — the UID and GID do. Practice verifying attributes with id, grep on system files, and chage to inspect expiration.

screens.title: UIDs and GIDs: what the kernel uses
screens.subtitle: Numeric identity is the truth; names are human-friendly labels

narration.text: A UID is a numeric identifier the kernel uses to record file ownership, process owners, and access decisions. A GID is the numeric identifier for a group. While humans interact with names like alice or developers, the kernel keeps only numbers. This distinction matters when systems share storage or when accounts are migrated. For example, if a user named devuser has UID 1001 on one server and UID 1005 on another, files created on the first host will appear to belong to the numeric owner when viewed on the second host — possibly mapped to a different username or shown as an unknown numeric owner. A concrete example: mounting a shared NFS export created by a user on Host A with UID 1001 on Host B where UID 1001 maps to nobody will break ownership expectations. A common misconception is assuming usernames alone control permissions; instead, ensure UID and GID alignment across hosts for shared resources. Key takeaway: treat UIDs and GIDs as stable identifiers in system design. When planning migrations or shared storage, establish a mapping policy or centralized identity management to avoid mismatches. How will you ensure UID consistency in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Numeric identity rules
keyIdea.text: Always think in terms of numeric IDs for ownership and access; plan for consistent UIDs/GIDs across systems that share data.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › UIDs and GIDs
Definition
UID: kernel-level numeric user identifier. GID: numeric group identifier used for group ownership.
Concrete example
User devuser has UID 1001 on Host A. If Host B has UID 1001 assigned to another account, the file ownership will not match the username when mounted over NFS.
Common mistake
Relying on usernames for permission checks rather than verifying numeric IDs across systems.
Key Takeaway

UIDs and GIDs are the authoritative owners. Plan for consistent mapping when sharing storage or migrating users.

Annotated notes
  • Kernel compares numbers; user and group names are for display.
  • Networked storage and NFS depend on matching IDs to preserve permissions.
  • Establish an ID allocation policy ahead of service and user provisioning.
Check your understanding
If a file shows numeric owner 1002 on one host, what should you verify on another host to determine the corresponding username?

screens.title: Primary vs Secondary Groups
screens.subtitle: How primary and supplementary groups determine file access

narration.text: Every user has a primary group and may belong to additional secondary groups. The primary group is the one recorded as the file group owner when the user creates new files, unless the parent directory has a setgid bit or other group behavior configured. Secondary groups grant extra permissions for shared resources. For example, a user in the dev_team secondary group can access project files owned by that group, while the user's primary group may be a personal group with the same name as the user. Creating a user with useradd -G dev_team appuser makes dev_team a secondary group; using usermod -aG dev_team adds a user to a group without removing other secondary groups. A common error is using usermod -G without -a, which replaces all secondary groups and can unintentionally revoke permissions. Practical verification steps include id username to list all group memberships and ls -l to see which group owns files. Takeaway: choose primary groups deliberately for default ownership, and use secondary groups for collaborative access. When changing a primary group use usermod -g so you do not inadvertently modify secondary group membership.

keyIdea.title: Group semantics
keyIdea.text: Primary group sets default file group owner; secondary groups provide additional access. Use usermod flags carefully to avoid replacing memberships.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Primary vs Secondary
Primary group
Typically a private group created with the username. Files you create will usually inherit this group as owner.
Secondary groups
Used for shared resources, project directories, and role-based access. Users can belong to multiple secondary groups.
Common mistake

Using usermod -G without -a will replace secondary groups and may remove needed access.

Visual comparison
Scenario: default file creation
Creator: alice, Primary group: alice. New files belong to group alice unless directory enforces setgid.
Scenario: project access
Alice added to dev_team as secondary group: membership lets her access dev_team-owned files.
Key Takeaway

Manage primary groups for default ownership and use secondary groups for shared permissions; append with -aG to avoid accidental removal.

screens.title: Creating system and regular users with useradd
screens.subtitle: Flags and meaning: -r, -s, -d, -c, -G

narration.text: Creating users with precise attributes prevents security gaps and simplifies later troubleshooting. The useradd tool accepts flags for system accounts, shells, home directories, comments, and secondary groups. Use -r to create a system account typically placed within a lower UID range; pair that with -s /sbin/nologin for non-interactive service users. The -d option sets a custom home directory when an application expects data in a particular place. The -c flag allows an administrative comment to describe purpose. To add secondary groups at creation use -G. For example, to create a web service account you might use useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin -d /var/www/mywebapp -c "My WebApp Service User" mywebapp and then verify attributes by running id mywebapp and grepping /etc/passwd. A common misconception is to omit -r and get a regular user with a login shell; that increases risk. Always verify after creation and adjust with usermod rather than editing system files directly. Takeaway: choose flags intentionally to match intended account behavior and reduce attack surface. Creating system and regular users with useradd means use precise useradd flags to create accounts that match their purpose and reduce accidental interactivity or incorrect ownership.. In practical terms, flags and meaning: -r, -s, -d, -c, -g. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Intentional creation
keyIdea.text: Use precise useradd flags to create accounts that match their purpose and reduce accidental interactivity or incorrect ownership.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Creating users
Flags and intent
  • -r creates a system account; often lower UID range and no interactive session.
  • -s sets the default shell; e.g., /sbin/nologin to prevent login.
  • -d sets a custom home directory for application data.
  • -c adds an administrative comment describing the account purpose.
  • -G assigns secondary groups at creation time.
Key Takeaway

Select flags to match account purpose; verify attributes after creation with id and grep.

Example commands
sudo useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin -d /var/www/mywebapp -c "My WebApp Service User" mywebapp
# Verify user creation
id mywebapp
grep mywebapp /etc/passwd
grep mywebapp /etc/shadow
Note: verify the user exists and check the shell and home directory fields in /etc/passwd. Use id to confirm UID and group membership.

screens.title: Modifying users and groups safely
screens.subtitle: usermod, groupadd, groupmod, and gpasswd patterns

narration.text: Making changes to users and groups should be done with the provided utilities to avoid inconsistencies. Use groupadd to create a new group, usermod to change a user’s primary group with -g, and usermod -aG to append secondary groups without removing existing memberships. The order matters: when you need to both change primary group and add secondary groups, add secondary groups first or use explicit append flags so you don't overwrite memberships. For group administration, groupmod changes group attributes and gpasswd manages group passwords and administrators. Avoid editing group files by hand; small mistakes can orphan users or groups. A concrete example: create devops_team with groupadd, then make jane_doe a member and change her primary group with sudo groupadd devops_team followed by sudo usermod -aG devops_team jane_doe and sudo usermod -g devops_team jane_doe if you need to change primary. A common misconception is thinking -G will append; without -a it replaces secondary groups. Always verify changes with id and grep to ensure the expected memberships are present. Final question: after adding a user to several groups, how will you confirm the user retains prior group memberships?

keyIdea.title: Safe modification
keyIdea.text: Use append flags and verify changes to avoid accidentally replacing a user's group membership when modifying accounts.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Modifying users
Common commands
  • groupadd name — create a new group for projects or roles.
  • groupmod — change a group's attributes; use carefully.
  • usermod -aG group user — append a secondary group.
  • usermod -g group user — change primary group.
  • gpasswd — manage group administrators or group passwords if used.
Misconception

Assuming usermod -G will add groups; without -a it replaces all secondary groups.

Example workflow
1) Create group: groupadd devops_team. 2) Add user as secondary: usermod -aG devops_team jane_doe. 3) Change primary if needed: usermod -g devops_team jane_doe. 4) Verify: id jane_doe.
Key Takeaway

Always verify group changes after modifying accounts and prefer tools over manual file edits to keep consistency.

screens.title: Understanding /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
screens.subtitle: What each file contains and why passwords are separated

narration.text: The /etc/passwd file stores account metadata: username, numeric UID, numeric GID, comment, home directory, and default shell. Historically it also stored password hashes, but modern systems place password hashes in /etc/shadow to restrict read access to root only. This separation prevents non-privileged users from obtaining hashed passwords and attempting offline cracking. A typical /etc/passwd entry includes colon-separated fields for identification and shell location but not the password hash. For troubleshooting, reading /etc/passwd helps locate a user's home directory and configured shell, while /etc/shadow contains sensitive password and aging information such as last change and expiration fields. A common mistake is attempting to change password hashes directly in /etc/shadow; always use passwd to ensure proper hashing and file integrity. Example: if a user's shell shows /sbin/nologin in /etc/passwd, that account is intentionally non-interactive. Takeaway: inspect passwd for account attributes and shadow only as root to investigate authentication and aging details. How would you check if an account is set to expire without reading raw hashes? Understanding /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow means /etc/passwd holds account metadata; /etc/shadow holds secure password hashes and aging info readable only by root.. In practical terms, what each file contains and why passwords are separated. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: File roles
keyIdea.text: /etc/passwd holds account metadata; /etc/shadow holds secure password hashes and aging info readable only by root.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › /etc/passwd & /etc/shadow
/etc/passwd
Contains username, UID, GID, comment, home directory, and default shell. It is world readable for name resolution.
/etc/shadow
Contains password hashes and aging fields and is readable only by root to protect sensitive hashes from unprivileged access.
Misconception

Editing /etc/shadow directly is dangerous; use passwd to change passwords to ensure correct hashing and permissions.

Example entries
alice:x:1001:1001:Alice:/home/alice:/bin/bash
# In /etc/shadow (root only)
alice:$6$...hashed...:18765:0:99999:7:::
Inspect /etc/passwd for shell and home. Use chage -l username to get aging and expiration information without viewing the raw hash directly.

screens.title: /etc/group, /etc/gshadow, and /etc/login.defs
screens.subtitle: Group metadata, secure group data, and system-wide defaults

narration.text: The /etc/group file maps group names to GIDs and lists group members. It is readable for name resolution. /etc/gshadow stores group passwords and administrators and is only readable by root for security. While group passwords are rarely used, gshadow lets administrators manage group administrators and group-specific secrets. /etc/login. defs controls default parameters for user creation such as UID/GID ranges, password aging defaults, and umask used during useradd operations. Understanding these files helps you enforce consistent policies across accounts. For example, setting system UID ranges in login. defs ensures system accounts are created with UIDs below a chosen threshold, keeping them separate from regular user ranges and avoiding accidental collisions. A common mistake is relying solely on useradd defaults without checking login. defs, which can lead to unexpected UID assignments. To troubleshoot membership issues, grep the group name to see member lists in /etc/group, and use gpasswd to safely change group administrators instead of direct edits. Takeaway: use these files to set organizational defaults and to audit group membership and policies securely. /etc/group, /etc/gshadow, and /etc/login.defs means /etc/group lists memberships; /etc/gshadow secures group credentials; /etc/login.defs defines defaults used when creating accounts.. In practical terms, group metadata, secure group data, and system-wide defaults. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Group files and defaults
keyIdea.text: /etc/group lists memberships; /etc/gshadow secures group credentials; /etc/login.defs defines defaults used when creating accounts.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Group files & defaults
/etc/group
Maps group names to GIDs and lists members. Use it to audit membership quickly.
/etc/gshadow
Stores group passwords and admin lists. Readable only by root and managed via gpasswd for safety.
/etc/login.defs
Defines system defaults for useradd including UID/GID ranges and password aging defaults. Adjust to enforce organizational policy.
Key Takeaway

Audit group membership in /etc/group, manage secure group settings via gpasswd and gshadow, and tune login.defs to ensure consistent user and system account ranges.

screens.title: Account lifecycle: expiration and locking
screens.subtitle: chage, passwd -l, and safe retirement of access

narration.text: Managing account lifecycle prevents stale or compromised access. The chage utility sets and shows password aging and expiration information; chage -E lets you set an expiration date for an account. For immediate suspension, passwd -l locks a user by disabling password authentication. Combined, these tools let you schedule decommissioning and react quickly to incidents. For example, set an account expiration 90 days from today with chage -E followed by the calculated date to ensure temporary project access is removed automatically. A common misconception is that deleting a user is always the safest step; deleting removes the account but leaves files owned by the numeric UID outside home directories. Instead, plan: lock the account first to deny access, locate externally-owned files by UID, reassign ownership or archive data, and then delete when safe. Verify account status with chage -l username and pwck or passwd -S to check lock status. Takeaway: prefer staged retirement—lock, reassign, then delete—to avoid orphaned access and data exposure. Account lifecycle: expiration and locking means lock or expire accounts first, reassign or clean external data, then delete to avoid orphaned ownership and unexpected access gaps.. In practical terms, chage, passwd -l, and safe retirement of access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stage before delete
keyIdea.text: Lock or expire accounts first, reassign or clean external data, then delete to avoid orphaned ownership and unexpected access gaps.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Account lifecycle
Expiration and locking
  • Use chage to set expiration dates and view aging information.
  • Use passwd -l to lock accounts immediately.
  • Verify with chage -l and passwd -S or getent passwd.
Best practice

Lock first, locate and reassign files, then delete. This staged approach avoids accidental data loss or orphaned ownership.

Quick commands
# Set an expiration date for john_doe
sudo chage -E YYYY-MM-DD john_doe

# Lock a user immediately
sudo passwd -l jane_doe

# Verify
chage -l alice
passwd -S alice
Use chage -l to review aging fields such as last changed, min and max days, and set expiration to automate retirement.

screens.title: Deleting users and handling orphaned files
screens.subtitle: userdel -r, implications, and reclaiming ownership

narration.text: Deleting a user removes the account entry, and with userdel -r you can remove the user's home directory and mail spool, but files outside that home will remain with the deleted numeric UID. This can leave orphaned ownership records that either map to no username or to a different user on another host. You must plan for this: locate files owned by a deleted UID with a find command that searches by numeric UID and then reassign ownership or archive them before removing the account. A practical approach is to compute the deleted UID, then run a targeted find such as find / -uid UID -exec chown newuser:newgroup {} \; to reassign ownership. Be careful to exclude system directories where ownership should remain as-is. A common misconception is thinking userdel -r removes all traces; it does not affect files outside the removed home directory. Takeaway: audit the filesystem for orphaned files, reassign as appropriate, and record actions in change logs so other administrators understand ownership changes. Deleting users and handling orphaned files means userdel -r removes home, but files elsewhere keep numeric uid ownership. find them by uid and reassign or archive as policy dictates.. In practical terms, userdel -r, implications, and reclaiming ownership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Orphaned files risk
keyIdea.text: userdel -r removes home, but files elsewhere keep numeric UID ownership. Find them by UID and reassign or archive as policy dictates.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Deleting users
What userdel -r does
Removes the account entry and, with -r, the user's home directory and mail spool, but not files elsewhere on the filesystem.
Common mistake

Assuming userdel -r purges all files owned by that account; it does not touch files outside the home.

Find and reassign
# Find files owned by a deleted UID and reassign
sudo find / -xdev -uid 1005 -exec chown newuser:newgroup {} \;

# Or archive first
sudo find / -xdev -uid 1005 -print0 | tar --null -T - -czf /root/orphaned-1005.tar.gz
Use -xdev to avoid crossing mountpoints unintentionally. Replace numeric UID with the deleted UID you observed from prior grep of /etc/passwd.

screens.title: Hands-on: creating dev_team, alice, bob, and deploy_svc
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step commands for the scenario

narration.text: We'll walk through the hands-on scenario from the chapter. The goal is to create a project group, two regular users who join it as a secondary group, and a system account for deployments. Start by creating the group with groupadd dev_team. Then create alice and bob with home directories and bash shells, adding them to dev_team as a secondary group so they share project resources. After creation, verify each account with id and by grepping /etc/passwd, and set an expiration date for alice with chage -E using a calculated date 90 days from today. Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Hands-on Activity
Planned steps
  1. Create dev_team group.
  2. Create alice and bob with homes and add to dev_team as secondary group.
  3. Create deploy_svc system account with no login and custom data directory.
  4. Set alice's expiration to 90 days from today.
  5. Verify every account with id and grep.
Key Takeaway

Follow the create-verify pattern and prepare directories before assigning them as home paths.

Commands (example)
# Step 1: Create the dev_team group
sudo groupadd dev_team

# Step 2: Create users alice and bob
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G dev_team alice
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G dev_team bob

# Step 3: Prepare and create deploy_svc
sudo mkdir -p /opt/deploy_data
sudo useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin -d /opt/deploy_data -c "Automated Deployment Service" deploy_svc

# Step 4: Set expiration for alice
# Calculate date: date -d "+90 days" +%Y-%m-%d
sudo chage -E YYYY-MM-DD alice

# Step 5: Verify
id alice
grep alice /etc/passwd
chage -l alice
grep dev_team /etc/group

screens.title: Service accounts and non-interactive shells
screens.subtitle: Why /sbin/nologin is preferred and how to choose home directories

narration.text: Service accounts require special handling to reduce attack surface and to keep service data organized. Prefer creating them as system accounts with a UID in the system range and set the shell to /sbin/nologin to explicitly block interactive login attempts while providing a clear message to any login attempt. This is generally better than using /bin/false because nologin returns a message and makes intent explicit for auditing. For home directories, choose paths that match application expectations: for web apps, /var/www or /srv/app_data; for deployment tools, /opt/deploy_data. Create directories before assigning them as home to avoid useradd failures or incorrect ownership. A common misconception is that system accounts should not have any home at all; in fact some services need a data directory even if interactive login is disabled. Takeaway: select shell and home intentionally to match service needs and to document purpose with the account comment. screens.title: Common mistakes and best practices
screens.subtitle: Inconsistent IDs, shell choices, and lifecycle errors to avoid

narration.text: Experienced administrators repeatedly see a few classes of avoidable mistakes. First, inconsistent UID/GID allocation across hosts creates permission and ownership confusion when mounting shared storage. Fix this by establishing a documented UID/GID map or employing centralized identity management. Second, misconfigured service accounts — for example giving a service a normal shell or forgetting to set -r — can open unnecessary login paths. Use /sbin/nologin and system UIDs to signal non-interactive accounts. Third, deletion without cleanup leaves orphaned files; follow a staged retirement process: lock first, find and reassign external files, then remove the account. Fourth, using usermod -G without -a strips secondary groups; always use -aG to append. Finally, rely on tools rather than editing passwd or group files by hand; utilities handle related files consistently and maintain file integrity. A concrete best practice: maintain a small document that records critical service UIDs and GIDs so new hosts can be aligned. Takeaway: enforce policies, verify after changes, and prefer tools and staged actions to avoid surprises. Top mistakes
  • Not aligning UIDs/GIDs across hosts serving shared storage.
  • Giving service accounts interactive shells or forgetting -r.
  • Deleting users without reassigning files outside home.
  • Using usermod -G without -a and unintentionally removing memberships.
Best practices
  • Document critical service UIDs/GIDs and sync them across systems.
  • Use /sbin/nologin and system UID ranges for non-interactive accounts.
  • Stage user retirement: lock, reassign/archive files, then delete.
  • Prefer useradd/usermod/gpasswd over manual file edits; verify with id and grep.
Key Takeaway

Policies and verification are your strongest tools. Prevent issues by documenting and confirming identity mappings and account attributes.

narration.text: Here are the key concepts to retain. First, UIDs and GIDs are numeric identifiers the kernel uses; ensure consistency across hosts when sharing storage. Second, primary groups set default file group ownership while secondary groups grant additional access; append secondary groups with -aG to avoid removing memberships. Third, use useradd flags like -r, -s, -d, -c, and -G intentionally to create accounts that match their purpose, especially for non-interactive service accounts. Each of these concepts supports reliable and secure account management. As a final reflection, when you next create a user or service account, consider what numeric ID it should have, which groups it needs, and whether it should be allowed to log in interactively.
